title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 34 (Criminal Liability for Mis-statements in Prospectus)

content.overview: Section 34 imposes criminal liability where a prospectus includes any statement which is untrue or misleading in form or context, or where any inclusion or omission is likely to mislead. Every person who authorises the issue of such prospectus is liable under section 447, subject to statutory defences of immateriality or reasonable belief.
content.glance: Untrue or misleading statement or likely-to-mislead inclusion/omission in a prospectus; liability of persons who authorise issue under s. 447; defences of immateriality or reasonable belief.
content.study:
Where a prospectus, issued, circulated or distributed under Chapter III, includes any statement which is untrue or misleading in form or context in which it is included, or where any inclusion or omission of any matter is likely to mislead, every person who authorises the issue of such prospectus is liable under section 447. A defence is available if the person proves that the statement or omission was immaterial, or that he had reasonable grounds to believe, and did up to the time of issue of the prospectus believe, that the statement was true or the inclusion or omission was necessary.

Case-law framing (batch 2 — prospectus cluster)
• Liability under s. 34 is statute-driven. It is not necessary to prove common-law deceit as in Derry v Peek in order to attract the section; the statute supplies the trigger (untrue or misleading statement / likely-to-mislead inclusion or omission) and the consequence (liability under s. 447).
• Derry v Peek (1889) 14 App Cas 337 (HL) remains the foundational authority on the common-law meaning of fraud in a prospectus context: fraud is proved when a false representation is made knowingly, or without belief in its truth, or recklessly careless whether it be true or false. Honest belief in truth, even if careless, is not deceit at common law. That standard illuminates the statutory “reasonable grounds to believe” defence under the proviso to s. 34, but does not replace the statutory test.
• Predecessor criminal provision: Companies Act, 1956, s. 63.
• Primary-report line-level verification of Indian Supreme Court applications of s. 34 / s. 447 in prospectus prosecutions remains open. Not COMPLETE_LOCKED.

sections.heading: Trigger
sections.body: Prospectus contains an untrue or misleading statement in form or context, or an inclusion/omission likely to mislead.

sections.heading: Persons Liable
sections.body: Every person who authorises the issue of such prospectus is liable under section 447.

sections.heading: Defences
sections.body: Defence if the statement/omission was immaterial, or the person had reasonable grounds to believe and did believe it was true or necessary.

provisions.title: Criminal liability for mis-statements in prospectus

examples.title: Misleading revenue figure
examples.body: A prospectus states inflated revenues. Persons who authorised its issue face s. 34 liability under s. 447 unless a statutory defence is made out.

examples.title: Reasonable belief defence
examples.body: A director authorised issue after independent verification that supported the statement. The reasonable-belief defence under s. 34 may apply.

hypotheticals.question: Is civil loss required for s. 34 liability?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 34 is criminal liability for misstatements; civil compensation is under s. 35.

hypotheticals.question: Does s. 34 require proof of common-law deceit as in Derry v Peek?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 34 is a statutory offence. Derry v Peek explains common-law fraud and illuminates the belief defence, but the trigger and consequence are supplied by the statute.

distinctions.title: Criminal liability (s. 34) vs civil liability (s. 35)
distinctions.right: Civil: compensation for loss from reliance on misleading prospectus

misconceptions.trap: Only the company is criminally liable for prospectus misstatements.
misconceptions.correction: Section 34 targets every person who authorises the issue, with liability under s. 447.

misconceptions.trap: Section 34 requires proof of common-law deceit under Derry v Peek.
misconceptions.correction: Section 34 is statute-driven. Derry v Peek informs the concept of fraud and belief but does not replace the statutory test.

cases.name: Derry v Peek
cases.point: At common law, fraud (deceit) in a prospectus representation is proved only where a false statement is made knowingly, or without belief in its truth, or recklessly careless whether it be true or false. Honest belief in the truth of the statement is a defence to deceit, even if the belief was formed carelessly.
cases.note: Foundational House of Lords authority on common-law deceit in a prospectus context. Illuminates the statutory reasonable-belief defence under the proviso to s. 34 but does not replace the statutory offence. Not a decision under the Companies Act, 2013. Primary-report line-level verification of subsequent Indian applications remains open.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 34 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify prospectus and misstatement/omission. II. Identify who authorised issue. III. Test statutory defences (immateriality / reasonable belief). IV. Apply s. 447. V. Distinguish from s. 35 civil route. VI. Conclude.

examTips: State the two statutory defences clearly.
Cite Derry v Peek for common-law fraud/belief; stress that s. 34 is statute-driven.

relatedJudgments.name: Derry v Peek
relatedJudgments.point: Common-law deceit in prospectus: knowledge, absence of belief, or reckless carelessness; honest belief is a defence to deceit.
